title: What Am I Supposed to Do With My Time?
theme: Time, eternity, understanding God, recognizing Christ, accepting the cross, and discovering how to serve God within the time we have been given
opening: I know my life has a beginning and an end. What I don't know is what I am supposed to do with everything in between.
prayer: Lord, You have placed eternity within my heart, yet I see only this small part of Your work. I want to understand so much, but even more than understanding You, I want to know You and remain close to You. Teach me not to fear what I cannot comprehend. Help me recognize the time You have given me and not waste it searching endlessly for answers that belong to You. When a cross comes that I do not understand, help me remain with You and allow You and Mary to bear it with me. Show me how to serve You in the life I have now, in the people before me, and in the ordinary moments of my days. I know I cannot see the whole story. Give me the grace to faithfully live the part You have given me. Amen.
body:
There are certain words of Jesus that I can read over and over again and still feel as though there is something I am missing. Today was one of those times. Jesus asks His disciples, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” They give Him the answers they have heard: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the ancient prophets. But then He changes the question. “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answers, “The Christ of God.”
I have always been impressed by this exchange, but I don't know that I have completely understood why. Jesus asks them who He is, Peter gives what seems to be the right answer, and then Jesus rebukes them and tells them not to tell anyone. Why? It reminds me of something else I have struggled to understand. During the Sorrowful Mysteries, there is a prayer asking Mary for the grace to always accept our cross, so that she and Jesus may bear it with us.
Accept my cross. I understand the words. But what does that really mean? Does accepting a cross mean accepting suffering? Does it mean I should not want something painful to change? Does it mean I am supposed to understand why it happened? These are the places where I can read the words again and again and feel that I understand part of them, but not the core. One of my greatest fears is not understanding enough.
Yet I also believe God prepares our hearts to understand things according to His timing. I can read, study, question and try to decipher, but sometimes clarity comes much later. Something I have read many times suddenly becomes different because perhaps I am finally in the place where I can hear it. Which makes today's first reading from Ecclesiastes almost perfect: “There is an appointed time for everything.” A time to be born and a time to die. A time to weep and a time to laugh. A time to mourn and a time to dance. A time to seek and a time to lose.
Then comes the line that I cannot stop thinking about: “He has made everything appropriate to its time, and has put the timeless into their hearts, without man's ever discovering, from beginning to end, the work which God has done.”
Maybe this is part of what I keep struggling against. I live completely within time. I was born. I am here now. One day I will die. My days move in one direction, and lately they seem to move incredibly fast. I cannot go backward. I cannot see very far forward. I experience my existence one moment after another, a tiny speck among all the people who have lived before me and all those who will come afterward. But God has put the timeless into our hearts.
How strange and beautiful that is. We live inside time while somehow yearning for something beyond it. We ask questions about eternity even though we cannot comprehend eternity. We want to understand the beginning and the end while standing somewhere in the middle. And Ecclesiastes tells us plainly that we will not discover, from beginning to end, all the work God has done. Maybe I have been asking myself to understand something I was never capable of seeing completely.
I think about God's existence and can only say that He has always been. Even that sentence feels inadequate because “always” is a word I understand through time. God remains a mystery to me, and perhaps He should. But my heart yearns for Him. And I realized something today: my heart yearns for God more than it yearns for understanding Him.
Maybe that matters, because Peter knew who Jesus was before Peter understood what that answer would mean. “You are the Christ of God.” Peter got that part right. But immediately afterward Jesus tells them that the Son of Man must suffer greatly, be rejected, be killed and on the third day be raised. Peter could recognize Christ without yet understanding the Cross.
Perhaps that is why Jesus' question is so different from the first one. “Who do the crowds say that I am?” asks what everyone else thinks. “But who do you say that I am?” asks something of my own heart. Maybe Jesus is not first asking me, “Do you understand everything about Me?” Maybe He is asking, “Who am I to you?” And I can answer that even while so much remains mysterious.
Then perhaps accepting my cross becomes a little clearer too. Maybe accepting the cross does not mean pretending suffering is good. It doesn't mean I wanted it. It doesn't mean something painful should not be changed when it can be changed, and it certainly doesn't mean I understand why it happened. Maybe accepting my cross sometimes simply means saying: This is where I am, Lord. I do not understand all of it, and I would not have chosen all of it, but I will not leave You here. And perhaps that is why the prayer asks Mary and Jesus to help bear it. We were never being asked to carry everything alone.
Still, I find myself wanting to know the master plan. Why this time? Why this life? Why these particular circumstances? What becomes of everything I do? But I cannot think that far ahead. From God's perspective, perhaps “ahead” isn't even the right word. I am the one living one day after another.
So maybe the question I can answer is much smaller: What am I supposed to do with the time I have been given?
That question matters to me because I do not want to waste it. My days go quickly. Years go quickly. I want to be of service to God during this little stretch between my birth and my death. I don't necessarily mean some enormous mission. Maybe service happens in much smaller ways than that. Loving someone. Forgiving someone. Helping someone. Writing something. Praying. Listening. Remaining faithful when I would rather retreat. Carrying a cross without allowing it to separate me from Christ.
Maybe there really is a time for all of it, and perhaps I don't have to understand how every moment fits into God's work from beginning to end. I only have to pay attention to the time I am in. Peter did not understand everything when he said, “The Christ of God.” Mary did not have every answer before she said yes to God. And I don't need to understand eternity before I begin living toward it.
I know who I want to follow. I know who my heart yearns for. Maybe faith is not seeing the entire story. Maybe it is knowing whom I am following through the part of the story I have been given. There is a time for everything. This is my time, and while I am here, I want it to belong to Him.
